selection_rule: top-k species by (n_distinct_proposers, n_members, stable sha256); representative = member with smallest sha256(pid)

selected.name: Topical Reference Self-Sufficiency
selected.instruction: Score how well the caption's humor stands on its own without relying on a topical, cultural, or celebrity reference as the primary comedic engine. A 10 means the caption is fully self-sufficient—any reference present is incidental to a joke that works on its own terms, or no reference is needed at all. A 0 means the caption's entire comedic value depends on recognizing a specific topical reference and removing it leaves nothing.
selected.rationale: The scorecard appears to reward topical references regardless of integration. Dense-low R41 ('easier to get than an N95 mask') and R53 ('his full 1200 stimulus') use the reference as the entire joke. Dense-high R25 embeds COVID references (masks, six feet) as secondary details inside a richer baseball scenario, and R40's ten-dollar-beer complaint is organic to the domestic situation.
member_names: Dark Humor And Escalation Of Stakes

selected.name: Speaker-role fidelity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the line sounds natural for a particular depicted speaker given that character’s role and situation; score 0 when no plausible depicted speaker could say it.
selected.rationale: R17 and R49 make the miniature-person device part of an office power exchange, while R13 and R30 provide lines with weakly defined speakers and situations.

selected.name: Non-template angle
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the association is surprising and individualized rather than a stock response; score 0 when it uses the first cliché suggested by the image.
selected.rationale: R17 uses a sinking-Venice association for the chandelier catch, while R38 gives a more elaborated inventory of rejected lighting fixtures.

selected.name: Payoff surprise
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the ending sharply redirects the reader toward an unexpected but coherent interpretation; score 0 when the punchline is an obvious first association or lacks a turn.
selected.rationale: R21, R30, and R60 deliver unexpected reframings of elevators, the moon, and shopping; R02 and R06 rely on more immediately predictable associations.

selected.name: Layered semantic convergence
selected.instruction: Score 10 when two or more meanings converge cleanly on the pictured situation; score 0 when the line has only one thin, literal reading.
selected.rationale: R18 combines extinction with the persistence of hats, while R59 connects the moon's face to an emoji and a broader cultural comparison.

selected.name: Petty-Stakes Emotional Grounding
selected.instruction: Score how specifically and relatably a depicted character is invested in a small, human-scale concern—petty grievance, minor inconvenience, domestic anxiety, social embarrassment—rather than the grand absurdity of the scene. A 10 means the character's emotional investment is vivid, relatable, and comically disproportionate to the surreal situation. A 0 means no specific emotional investment is conveyed.
selected.rationale: Dense-high entries ground surreal scenes in petty emotions: R40's outrage over ten-dollar beer charges amid a living-room baseball game; R54's recursive disappointment about a wish gone wrong; R56's bear complaining about the hardship of river-fishing with your mouth. These granular emotional stakes separate great entries from merely clever ones.

selected.name: Setup-to-Payoff Register Shift
selected.instruction: Score how effectively the caption's opening words set up one expectation—emotional, tonal, or topical—and then deliver the payoff in a deliberately different register. A 10 means the gap between setup and payoff registers is wide and surprising yet perfectly coherent. A 0 means the setup leads predictably and linearly to its conclusion with no tonal pivot.
selected.rationale: Dense-high entries frequently pivot between registers mid-caption: R25 opens as COVID commentary but lands as casual baseball banter; R42 opens as a dramatic rescue line but reveals it is about dinner; R54 opens with mutual disappointment but pivots to a wish-gone-wrong backstory. Dense-low R24 ('well this is a new phase') never shifts register at all.

selected.name: Conversational punch timing
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the wording has a natural setup and lands its strongest turn at the end; score 0 when it is awkwardly phrased, overexplained, or lacks a punch.
selected.rationale: R10 delays the reveal of who is firing the employee, while R21 ends on the concrete surprise of being charged for beer already in the refrigerator.

selected.name: Secondary-detail leverage
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the humor depends on supporting props, background details, setting, or secondary characters as well as the central anomaly; score 0 when all such details are ignored.
selected.rationale: R20 uses the catcher’s mask and distancing behavior, R57 uses the room’s implied neighbors, and R58 uses the sheep’s visual similarity and a cotton bale.

selected.name: Freshness over cliché
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar phrase, reference, or association is materially twisted into a new comic idea; score 0 when it reproduces a stock expression with minimal alteration.
selected.rationale: R18, R37, R47, and R51 draw on familiar evolution, lunar, botanical, and sinking-related associations, making cliché resistance a useful distinction.

selected.name: Deadpan Underreaction To Surreal Danger
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the speaker treats a highly dangerous, bizarre, or impossible situation as a mundane, bureaucratic, or trivial inconvenience. Score 0 if the speaker reacts with shock or directly addresses the impossibility of the situation.
selected.rationale: The dense model values a casual tone in the face of absurdity. R02 (setting up the net for a cannon) and R44 (arriving early as if magic equals speed) contrast with the scorecard's preference for straightforward observations.

selected.name: Generic-prior obvious idiom
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption relies on the single most obvious idiom, pun, or literal interpretation directly invited by the visual elements of the scene. Do not judge whether the joke is clever or well-executed.
selected.rationale: General models often over-reward the consensus 'first-thought' reading of an image because it perfectly aligns text and image. R10 ('elephant in the room') and R23 ('downsizing') are the most predictable puns for their respective cartoons.
upstream_parent_all_members: position in the entry stream for the cartoon

selected.name: House-style tonal register
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses plain, restrained, everyday conversational diction and understated social framing; do not judge whether that register suits the cartoon.
selected.rationale: A publication's recurring register can imprint captions with dry understatement and ordinary workplace or domestic diction, independently of cartoon-specific merit, while register can also affect contest suitability. Examples include R03, R17, and R42.

selected.name: Generic caption polish
selected.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the caption has compact, complete, immediately legible setup-punch packaging familiar from generic caption examples; do not judge whether it is funny or apt.
selected.rationale: Well-formed caption-shaped language is easy for a general-purpose prior to recognize without requiring contest-specific taste. R03, R20, R32, and R56 use concise, self-contained conventional joke formats.

selected.name: Transcription artifacts
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption exhibits catalog or transcription conventions such as lowercase starts, omitted terminal punctuation, ellipses, doubled hyphens, or spacing quirks; judge only visible text, not whether the caption is good.
selected.rationale: Lowercase presentation in R03, ellipses in R04, and doubled hyphens in R29 and R39 may come from compilation conventions rather than the entrant's wording or cartoon-specific quality.

selected.name: Topical news cycle reference
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption explicitly names or directly references a specific contemporary real-world entity, person, product, or event (e.g., 'n95 mask', 'stimulus', 'trump'). Do not judge if the reference is funny or apt, only how specific and time-bound the named entity is.
selected.rationale: Topical references are artifacts of the submission timing and may impress a scorecard looking for cleverness, but they are not inherent qualities of the caption for that specific cartoon (e.g., R24, R28).
upstream_parent_all_members: news cycle at the moment of the contest

selected.name: Extreme conversational brevity
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption is extremely short, abandoning any narrative setup to deliver a quick, blunt conversational response (e.g., 'chicken or rabbit'). Do not judge if brevity makes it a good caption.
selected.rationale: Very short captions might be scored highly by dense models for punchiness, but they often rely on the weakest connection to the drawing, mimicking a laconic style rather than a strong premise (e.g., R12, R49).

selected.name: Pun and idiom density
selected.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the caption relies on homophones, double meanings, transformed idioms, or concentrated wordplay; do not judge whether the wordplay is clever.
selected.rationale: Wordplay density is an easily detected lexical channel that need not track cartoon-specific success. Examples include “ewe” repetition in R17, fishing “sconces” and “keeper” in R21, “spare ribs” in R25, and “roots” in R46.

selected.name: Practiced caption compression
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the line is compressed caption-native dialogue that assumes the drawing, omits explanation, and delivers one economical beat; do not judge whether the compression is effective.
selected.rationale: A serial entrant's familiarity with the format can leave disciplined brevity and refusal to narrate the image, while that same practice may also improve genuine writing skill. Compact examples include R03, R07, and R17.
upstream_parent_all_members: author's practice in the caption format

selected.name: Bureaucratic or corporate jargon usage
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption uses specific corporate, bureaucratic, or administrative terminology (e.g., 'downsizing', 'litigation', 'human resources'). Do not judge if it fits the drawing well.
selected.rationale: Using corporate speak to contrast with an absurd visual is a very common contest template that mimics the magazine's historical style but is not inherently a better contest entry (e.g., R13, R02).

selected.name: Verbose conversational filler
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption uses spoken-style filler words (e.g., 'wow', 'sure', 'well', 'i guess') or conversational run-on phrasing to set up the punchline, adding words that do not change the core joke. Do not judge if the phrasing is good.
selected.rationale: Serial entrants often know that caption contest jokes require a specific spoken rhythm, but a dense model might discount excessive verbosity that doesn't add to the visual gag (e.g., R34, R42).
